claims.source: Imprinted X-inactivation silences genes exclusively on the paternally-inherited X-chromosome and is a paradigm of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in mammals.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established fact stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: In maternal-null (Eedm-/-) but not zygotic-null (Eed-/-) early embryos, the maternal X-chromosome ectopically induced Xist and underwent inactivation.
claims.source: In maternal-null (Eedm-/-) but not zygotic-null (Eed-/-) early embryos, the maternal X-chromosome ectopically induced Xist and underwent inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH data presented in Figures 3-7.

claims.claim: Eedm-/- females subsequently stochastically silenced Xist from one of the two X-chromosomes and displayed random X-inactivation.
claims.source: Eedm-/- females subsequently stochastically silenced Xist from one of the two X-chromosomes and displayed random X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data showing mosaic patterns of Xist expression in Eedm-/- blastocysts (Figures 6-7).

claims.claim: The effect of maternal EED loss was exacerbated in embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic EED (Eedmz-/-).
claims.source: This effect was exacerbated in embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic EED (Eedmz-/-), suggesting that zygotic EED can also contribute to the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data showing greater paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedmz-/- compared to Eedm-/- embryos (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Zygotic EED can contribute to the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.source: This effect was exacerbated in embryos lacking both maternal and zygotic EED (Eedmz-/-), suggesting that zygotic EED can also contribute to the onset of imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos showing differential effects on X-inactivation.

claims.claim: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos.
claims.source: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2 and only undergo random X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of Xist RNA coating patterns in Eedm-/- mouse embryos with published data on human embryos, and RNA-Seq data showing lack of PRC2 expression in human oocytes (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Human embryos lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2.
claims.source: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2 and only undergo random X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data from human oocytes showing negligible expression of core PRC2 genes (Figure 8A).

claims.claim: Human embryos only undergo random X-inactivation.
claims.source: Xist expression dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble that of early human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2 and only undergo random X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is based on published literature cited in the manuscript (Okamoto et al., 2011; Petropoulos et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Expression of PRC2 in the oocyte and transmission of the gene products to the embryo may dictate the occurrence of imprinted X-inactivation in mammals.
claims.source: Thus, expression of PRC2 in the oocyte and transmission of the gene products to the embryo may dictate the occurrence of imprinted X-inactivation in mammals.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the comparison of mouse and human oocyte PRC2 expression and the phenotypes of maternal EED mutants.

claims.claim: Imprinted X-inactivation results in the silencing of genes exclusively on the paternal X-chromosome and initiates during preimplantation embryogenesis.
claims.source: Imprinted X-inactivation results in the silencing of genes exclusively on the paternal X-chromosome and initiates during preimplantation embryogenesis (Huynh and Lee, 2003; Mak et al., 2004; Monk and Kathuria, 1977; Okamoto et al., 2004; Takagi and Sasaki, 1975).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X is stably maintained in the extraembryonic lineage but reversed in the embryonic lineage.
claims.source: In later stage embryos, imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X is stably maintained in the extraembryonic lineage but reversed in the embryonic lineage (Harper et al., 1982; Mak et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Takagi and Sasaki, 1975; West et al., 1977), which subsequently undergoes random inactivation of either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome (Lyon, 1961).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The embryonic lineage subsequently undergoes random inactivation of either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome.
claims.source: In later stage embryos, imprinted X-inactivation of the paternal-X is stably maintained in the extraembryonic lineage but reversed in the embryonic lineage (Harper et al., 1982; Mak et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Takagi and Sasaki, 1975; West et al., 1977), which subsequently undergoes random inactivation of either the maternal or the paternal X-chromosome (Lyon, 1961).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Both imprinted and random X-inactivation are prefaced by the expression of X-linked non-protein coding Xist RNA from the prospective inactive-X.
claims.source: Both imprinted and random X-inactivation are prefaced by the expression of X-linked non-protein coding Xist RNA from the prospective inactive-X (Kay et al., 1994; Penny et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: During imprinted X-inactivation in the mouse embryo, Xist is expressed at the two-cell stage and the RNA visibly begins to coat the paternal-X at the four-cell stage.
claims.source: During imprinted X-inactivation in the mouse embryo, Xist is expressed at the two-cell stage and the RNA visibly begins to coat the paternal-X at the four-cell stage (Kalantry et al., 2009; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The progressive accumulation of Xist RNA coincides with the gradual and stereotyped silencing of paternal X-linked genes that is only completed after the blastocyst stage of embryogenesis.
claims.source: The progressive accumulation of Xist RNA coincides with the gradual and stereotyped silencing of paternal X-linked genes that is only completed after the blastocyst stage of embryogenesis (Kalantry et al., 2009; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Coincident with Xist RNA coating, Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) proteins and the PRC2-catalyzed chromatin mark histone H3K27me3 accumulate on the inactive-X, correlating with the silencing of X-linked genes.
claims.source: Coincident with Xist RNA coating, Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) proteins and the PRC2-catalyzed chromatin mark histone H3K27me3 accumulate on the inactive-X, correlating with the silencing of X-linked genes (Mak et al., 2004; Okamoto et al., 2004; Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The mis-expression of Xist results in the concomitant accumulation of PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3.
claims.source: Moreover, the mis-expression of Xist results in the concomitant accumulation of PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 (de la Cruz et al., 2005; Kohlmaier et al., 2004; Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003), suggesting that Xist RNA directly or indirectly recruits PRC2 to the inactive-X.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Xist RNA directly or indirectly recruits PRC2 to the inactive-X.
claims.source: Moreover, the mis-expression of Xist results in the concomitant accumulation of PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 (de la Cruz et al., 2005; Kohlmaier et al., 2004; Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003), suggesting that Xist RNA directly or indirectly recruits PRC2 to the inactive-X.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations cited in the literature.

claims.claim: PRC2 has been suggested to contribute to the establishment of X-inactivation.
claims.source: PRC2 has thus been suggested to contribute to the establishment of X-inactivation (Plath et al., 2003; Silva et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is based on published literature.

claims.claim: Post-implantation female mouse embryos mutant for the Polycomb gene Eed fail to maintain silencing of paternal X-linked genes during imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.source: Consistent with a role for PRC2 in X-inactivation, we and others previously showed that post-implantation female mouse embryos mutant for the Polycomb gene Eed fail to maintain silencing of paternal X-linked genes during imprinted X-inactivation (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors and others, as cited.

claims.claim: EED is a non-catalytic component of the PRC2 complex.
claims.source: EED is a non-catalytic component of the PRC2 complex, but EED binding to the PRC2 enzyme EZH2 is required for the full methyltransferase activity of EZH2 (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: EED binding to the PRC2 enzyme EZH2 is required for the full methyltransferase activity of EZH2.
claims.source: EED is a non-catalytic component of the PRC2 complex, but EED binding to the PRC2 enzyme EZH2 is required for the full methyltransferase activity of EZH2 (Cao et al., 2002; Czermin et al., 2002; Kuzmichev et al., 2002; Müller et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: When EED is mutated other core PRC2 proteins are degraded and the histone H3K27me3 mark is lost.
claims.source: When EED is mutated other core PRC2 proteins are degraded and the histone H3K27me3 mark is lost (Montgomery et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: EED is an essential component of PRC2 and EED function is canonically equated with H3K27me3 catalysis.
claims.source: Thus, EED is an essential component of PRC2 and EED function is canonically equated with H3K27me3 catalysis (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Montgomery et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.source: Although Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain imprinted X-inactivation, the mutant embryos initiate imprinted X-inactivation properly (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors, as cited.

claims.claim: Eed-/- embryos initiate imprinted X-inactivation properly.
claims.source: Although Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain imprinted X-inactivation, the mutant embryos initiate imprinted X-inactivation properly (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Kalantry et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors, as cited.

claims.claim: Eed-/- embryos inherit maternal EED protein that is present in the oocyte.
claims.source: A potential answer for this difference is that Eed-/- embryos inherit maternal EED protein that is present in the oocyte (Kalantry and Magnuson, 2006; Plath et al., 2003; Shumacher et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations and tested in this study.

claims.claim: The presence of maternally-derived EED protein could explain the absence of a defect in establishing imprinted X-inactivation in Eed-/- embryos.
claims.source: The presence of maternally-derived EED protein could explain the absence of a defect in establishing imprinted X-inactivation in Eed-/- embryos.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the study.

claims.claim: Maternal control of imprinted X-inactivation would be consistent with a transgenerational epigenetic effect that underlies genomic imprinting.
claims.source: Such maternal control of imprinted X-inactivation would also be consistent with a transgenerational epigenetic effect that underlies genomic imprinting (Barlow, 2011; Ferguson-Smith and Bourc'his, 2018; Lee and Bartolomei, 2013; van Otterdijk and Michels, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on established concepts of genomic imprinting, supported by citations.

claims.claim: PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 are first enriched on the prospective inactive paternal X-chromosome in the early mouse embryo at the 8–16 cell morula stage.
claims.source: PRC2 proteins and H3K27me3 are first enriched on the prospective inactive paternal X-chromosome in the early mouse embryo at the 8–16 cell morula stage (Okamoto et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos are in the process of silencing paternal X-linked genes and establishing imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.source: We assessed the accumulation of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA by immunofluorescence (IF) combined with RNA fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) in wild-type (WT) embryonic day (E) 3.5 blastocyst embryos (Cloutier et al., 2018; Hinten et al., 2016), which are in the process of silencing paternal X-linked genes and establishing imprinted X-inactivation (Borensztein et al., 2017; Namekawa et al., 2010; Patrat et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos, females displayed coincident accumulation of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA in a vast majority of the nuclei (72–100%).
claims.source: As expected, females displayed coincident accumulation of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA in a vast majority of the nuclei (72–100%).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF/FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos, males lacked enrichment of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA.
claims.source: Males, by contrast, lacked such enrichment (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF/FISH data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Genotypically null Eed-/- embryos inherit oocyte-derived maternal EED protein.
claims.source: Together, the results in Figure 1 suggest that genotypically null Eed-/- embryos inherit oocyte-derived maternal EED protein and that expression of EED transitions from maternal to zygotic at or slightly before the blastocyst stage.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from IF data showing EED and H3K27me3 enrichment in some embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: Expression of EED transitions from maternal to zygotic at or slightly before the blastocyst stage.
claims.source: Together, the results in Figure 1 suggest that genotypically null Eed-/- embryos inherit oocyte-derived maternal EED protein and that expression of EED transitions from maternal to zygotic at or slightly before the blastocyst stage.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from IF data showing variable EED and H3K27me3 enrichment patterns in embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: There is no bias in the sex ratio or genotype of embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses.
claims.source: Embryos from 12 litters showed no statistical difference in the distribution of Eed+/- and Eed-/- male or female embryos (p>0.05), suggesting that the intermediate class of 23 embryos in Figure 1A are likely a mixture of Eed+/- or Eed-/- embryos.
claims.evidence: This is supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 2-cell embryos exhibited similar levels of EED and H3K27me3.
claims.source: Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 2-cell embryos exhibited similar levels of EED and H3K27me3, whereas Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos were devoid of both EED and H3K27me3 (Figures 2A, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- 2-cell embryos were devoid of both EED and H3K27me3.
claims.source: Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 2-cell embryos exhibited similar levels of EED and H3K27me3, whereas Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos were devoid of both EED and H3K27me3 (Figures 2A, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The 2-cell embryo harbors only maternally-derived EED and H3K27me3.
claims.source: These data are consistent with the 2-cell embryo harboring only maternally-derived EED and H3K27me3.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- 2-cell embryos lack EED and H3K27me3 while Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos have similar levels.

claims.claim: Zygotic Eed expression begins at or slightly before the 4-cell stage.
claims.source: Four-cell embryos displayed a similar pattern to 2-cell embryos, although a subset of Eedfl/- / Eed-/- ~4-cell embryos displayed reduced EED and H3K27me3 levels, consistent with expression of zygotic EED beginning at or slightly before this stage and its failure in Eed-/- embryos (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from IF quantification data showing reduced EED and H3K27me3 in a subset of Eedfl/- / Eed-/- 4-cell embryos (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: At the ~8-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos showed highly variable EED and H3K27me3 levels.
claims.source: At the ~8-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos showed highly variable EED and H3K27me3 levels, suggesting further differentiation of the two genotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Eedm-/- ~8-cell embryos displayed higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the corresponding Eedmz-/- embryos.
claims.source: In agreement with increasing zygotic Eed expression, Eedm-/- ~8-cell embryos displayed higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the corresponding Eedmz-/- embryos (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: By the ~16-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos were clearly separated into two categories based on EED levels.
claims.source: By the ~16-cell stage, Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos were clearly separated into two categories. One group had statistically lower levels of EED, while the other group was statistically indistinguishable from Eedfl/fl embryos (Figures 2B, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claims.claim: The likely genotypes of the two groups of ~16-cell Eedfl/- / Eed-/- embryos are Eed-/- and Eedfl/-, respectively.
claims.source: Therefore, the likely genotypes of the two groups are Eed-/- and Eedfl/-, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential EED levels observed in the two groups of embryos.

claims.claim: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos continued to display higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the Eedmz-/- embryos.
claims.source: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos continued to display higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the Eedmz-/- embryos, but nevertheless harbored significantly lower EED and H3K27me3 levels than Eedfl/fl embryos (Figures 2B, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claims.claim: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos harbored significantly lower EED and H3K27me3 levels than Eedfl/fl embryos.
claims.source: Eedm-/- 16-cell embryos continued to display higher levels of EED and H3K27me3 than the Eedmz-/- embryos, but nevertheless harbored significantly lower EED and H3K27me3 levels than Eedfl/fl embryos (Figures 2B, C and D; Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF quantification data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D.

claims.claim: Maternally-derived EED starts declining at ~4-cell stage but is still present at the 16-cell stage.
claims.source: Maternally-derived EED starts declining at ~4-cell stage but is still present at the 16-cell stage.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data plotted across developmental stages (Figure 2E).

claims.claim: Zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage.
claims.source: Conversely, while zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage, zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos, suggesting that EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data and comparison of different genotypes (Figure 2E, F).

claims.claim: Zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos.
claims.source: Conversely, while zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage, zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos, suggesting that EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data and comparison of different genotypes (Figure 2E, F).

claims.claim: EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein.
claims.source: Conversely, while zygotic Eed transcription initiates at ~4-cell stage, zygotic EED levels are still low in ~16-cell embryos, suggesting that EED in WT Eedfl/fl 16-cell embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically generated protein (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the EED fluorescence intensity data and comparison of different genotypes (Figure 2E, F).

claims.claim: A subset of X-linked genes was expressed more robustly from the paternal allele relative to the maternal allele in Eedfl/- and Eed-/- female embryos compared to Eedfl/fl embryos.
claims.source: A subset of X-linked genes was expressed more robustly from the paternal allele relative to the maternal allele in Eedfl/- and Eed-/- female embryos compared to Eedfl/fl embryos (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Paternal X-linked gene expression was not significantly higher in Eed-/- blastocysts compared to Eedfl/- or Eedfl/fl female embryos.
claims.source: However, when the allelic expression ratio of all X-linked genes in Figure 3A was averaged, paternal X-linked gene expression was not significantly higher in Eed-/- blastocysts compared to Eedfl/- (p = 0.72) or Eedfl/fl (p = 0.76) female embryos (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: X-linked genes were expressed predominantly from the maternal allele in Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- female blastocysts.
claims.source: X-linked genes were expressed predominantly from the maternal allele in all three genotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: The ratio of maternal:paternal X-linked gene expression in Eed-/- female blastocysts was broadly similar to that in Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- embryos.
claims.source: Thus, the ratio of maternal:paternal X-linked gene expression in Eed-/- female blastocysts was broadly similar to that in Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- embryos.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Pyrosequencing did not detect any significant changes in maternal:paternal allelic expression of Xist, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 in hybrid Eed-/- vs. Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- blastocysts.
claims.source: We did not detect any significant changes in maternal:paternal allelic expression in hybrid Eed-/- vs. Eedfl/fl and Eedfl/- blastocysts (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Xist was expressed predominantly from the paternal allele in Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- female blastocysts.
claims.source: Whereas Xist was expressed predominantly from the paternal allele, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 were preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in all three genotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 were preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- female blastocysts.
claims.source: Whereas Xist was expressed predominantly from the paternal allele, Rnf12, Atrx, and Pgk1 were preferentially expressed from the maternal allele in all three genotypes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Pyrosequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Xist RNA coating and Rnf12 expression in female Eed-/- embryos did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl blastocysts.
claims.source: Xist RNA coating and Rnf12 expression in female Eed-/- embryos did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl blastocysts (Figure 3D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claims.claim: Both Eedfl/fl and Eed-/- female blastocysts displayed Xist RNA coating of one X-chromosome and Rnf12 expression from the other X-chromosome in a majority of the cells.
claims.source: Both sets of embryos displayed Xist RNA coating of one X-chromosome and Rnf12 expression from the other X-chromosome in a majority of the cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3D and F.

claims.claim: Male Eed-/- or Eed+/- embryos did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl embryos in their Rnf12 expression patterns.
claims.source: Male Eed-/- or Eed+/- embryos also did not differ significantly from Eedfl/fl embryos in their Rnf12 expression patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: By three independent assays – allele-specific RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH – zygotic Eed expression appears to be largely dispensable for the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.source: Thus, by three independent assays – allele-specific RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH – zygotic Eed expression appears to be largely dispensable for the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH experiments.

claims.claim: Eedm-/- blastocysts exhibited a small percentage of nuclei with H3K27me3 enrichment coinciding with the Xist RNA coat.
claims.source: Eedm-/- blastocysts exhibited a small percentage of nuclei with H3K27me3 enrichment coinciding with the Xist RNA coat (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF/RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Eedmz-/- blastocysts lacked all overlapping accumulation of H3K27me3 with the Xist RNA coat.
claims.source: Eedmz-/- blastocysts, on the other hand, lacked all such overlapping accumulation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by IF/RNA FISH data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: H3K27me3 enrichment on the Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- blastocysts is likely due to the expression of zygotic Eed in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- embryos.
claims.source: H3K27me3 enrichment on the Xist RNA-coated X-chromosome in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- blastocysts is likely due to the expression of zygotic Eed in Eedm-/- but not Eedmz-/- embryos (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos and the EED expression data in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The RNA-Seq data revealed a relative increase in paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
claims.source: Strikingly, the RNA-Seq data revealed a relative increase in paternal X-linked gene expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos (Figure 4B and C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Supplementary file 2 and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: Eedmz-/- embryos appeared to express paternal X-linked genes to a greater degree compared to Eedm-/- embryos.
claims.source: Furthermore, Eedmz-/- embryos appeared to express paternal X-linked genes to a greater degree compared to Eedm-/- embryos (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The difference in average allelic expression between Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos did not reach statistical significance (p=0.14).
claims.source: When allelic expression ratios of all X-linked genes in Figure 4B were averaged, however, the difference between Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos did not reach statistical significance (p=0.14) (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Paternal X-linked genes significantly increased in expression in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
claims.source: Whereas paternal X-linked genes significantly increased in expression, maternal X-linked gene expression decreased in Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos compared to Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, and Eed-/- embryos.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The Inoue et al. study did not directly demonstrate when imprinted X-inactivation switches to random X-inactivation and whether loss of zygotic Eed would result in a similar outcome.
claims.source: Although in agreement with our conclusions, the study did not directly demonstrate when imprinted X-inactivation switches to random X-inactivation and whether loss of zygotic Eed would result in a similar outcome.
claims.evidence: This is a critique of the Inoue et al. study.

results.result: The study demonstrates that EED expression transitions from maternal to zygotic during early embryogenesis. At the 2-cell stage, embryos harbor only maternally-derived EED and H3K27me3, with zygotic Eed transcription initiating at the ~4-cell stage. By the ~16-cell stage, EED in wild-type embryos is a combination of maternally-derived and zygotically-generated protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C50 are well-supported by immunofluorescence quantification data across developmental stages (Figure 2). The systematic comparison of Eedfl/fl, Eedfl/-, Eed-/-, Eedm-/-, and Eedmz-/- embryos at 2-, 4-, 8-, and 16-cell stages provides clear evidence for the temporal dynamics of maternal vs. zygotic EED expression. The statistical analyses and fluorescence intensity measurements support the conclusions about the transition timing.

results.result: Zygotic Eed expression is largely dispensable for the initiation and establishment of imprinted X-inactivation. Three independent assays (allele-specific RNA-Seq, Pyrosequencing, and RNA FISH) show that Eed-/- female blastocysts maintain predominantly maternal X-linked gene expression and paternal Xist expression, similar to wild-type embryos.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C61 are supported by convergent evidence from multiple orthogonal techniques (RNA-Seq in Figure 3A-B, Pyrosequencing in Figure 3C, and RNA FISH in Figure 3D-F). The consistency across methods strengthens the conclusion. Statistical analyses show no significant differences in X-linked gene expression patterns between Eed-/- and control embryos, supporting the dispensability of zygotic Eed for initiation of imprinted X-inactivation.

results.result: Maternal EED is required for proper initiation of imprinted X-inactivation. Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos show ectopic Xist induction from the maternal X-chromosome, increased paternal X-linked gene expression, and decreased maternal X-linked gene expression. Eedmz-/- embryos show more severe defects than Eedm-/- embryos, indicating that zygotic EED can contribute to silencing a subset of X-linked genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C82 are strongly supported by RNA-Seq (Figure 4B-D), Pyrosequencing (Figure 4E), and IF/RNA FISH data (Figure 4A). The comparison between Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos provides evidence for both maternal and zygotic EED contributions. Statistical significance is demonstrated for key comparisons (p<0.05), and the mechanistic interpretation linking maternal PRC2 to Xist repression is supported by published H3K27me3 ChIP-Seq data at the Xist locus.

results.result: Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos can resolve ectopic Xist expression and some survive to birth. Most nuclei in mutant female blastocysts display a single Xist RNA coat, though a subset shows coating of both X-chromosomes. Male Eedmz-/- embryos fall into two classes: well-developed embryos with few Xist-coated nuclei and underdeveloped embryos with high proportions of Xist-coated nuclei. Significantly more Eedm-/- females than males survive to birth (p=0.02).
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C97 are supported by RNA FISH data (Figure 5A-B) and breeding data (Figure 5C). The observation of two morphological classes of Eedmz-/- male embryos with different Xist coating frequencies provides evidence for adaptive resolution. The sex ratio difference in live births is statistically significant and suggests sex-specific differences in resolving ectopic Xist expression. However, the mechanism of resolution is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos switch from imprinted to random X-inactivation. Allele-specific Xist RNA FISH shows that in early (3-16 cell) Eedm-/- female embryos, most cells express Xist from both X-chromosomes, while male embryos express Xist from the sole maternal X-chromosome. By the blastocyst stage, most female cells display mosaic Xist expression from either the maternal or paternal X-chromosome, characteristic of random X-inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C120 are strongly supported by allele-specific Xist RNA FISH data (Figures 6-7). The temporal progression from biallelic Xist expression in early embryos to monoallelic mosaic expression in blastocysts provides direct evidence for the switch from imprinted to random X-inactivation. The allele-specific FISH technique is validated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1, strengthening confidence in the results.

results.result: The Xist expression pattern in Eedm-/- mouse embryos resembles that of human embryos, which lack oocyte-derived maternal PRC2. Human oocytes express core PRC2 genes (Eed, Ezh2, Ezh1, Suz12) at negligible levels compared to mouse oocytes. This difference may explain why human embryos undergo only random X-inactivation while mouse embryos undergo imprinted X-inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 are supported by RNA-Seq data comparing PRC2 gene expression in mouse and human oocytes (Figure 8A) and by comparison with published data on human embryo Xist expression patterns. The correlation between absence of maternal PRC2 and random X-inactivation in both Eedm-/- mouse embryos and human embryos is compelling. However, the causal relationship is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The early mouse embryo has an X-chromosome counting mechanism that ensures a single X-chromosome remains active regardless of parent of origin. This mechanism has been previously proposed based on studies of androgenetic and parthenogenetic embryos, and the current data from Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos support this model.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C136 are supported by the observation that Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos can resolve ectopic Xist expression to achieve monoallelic expression in females and loss of expression in males. The comparison with published data on androgenetic and parthenogenetic embryos strengthens the argument. However, the molecular mechanism of counting is not elucidated, and the conclusion relies heavily on inference from phenotypic observations.

results.result: The resolution of ectopic Xist expression in Eedm-/- embryos may involve silencing of Rnf12 on both X-chromosomes due to Xist RNA coating, leading to loss of Xist induction, followed by random X-inactivation in females. This mechanism is proposed based on the known requirement of maternal Rnf12 for Xist induction and the observation that Rnf12 is rapidly silenced upon Xist coating.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 are largely speculative. While C137-C138 are supported by published literature, C139-C141 are mechanistic proposals not directly tested in this study. The model is plausible and consistent with the data, but lacks direct experimental validation. RNA FISH shows loss of Rnf12 expression in cells with Xist coating of both Xs, but the temporal dynamics and causal relationships are not established.

results.result: Zygotic EED contributes to imprinted X-inactivation, with Eedmz-/- embryos showing greater paternal X-linked gene expression than Eedm-/- embryos. Two alternative interpretations are proposed: zygotic EED may preferentially install H3K27me3 at the maternal Xist locus to prevent its expression, or it may maintain silencing of paternal X-linked genes that have already initiated inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 is supported by RNA-Seq data showing significant differences between Eedm-/- and Eedmz-/- embryos (p=0.02). However, C124-C127 are speculative mechanistic interpretations not directly tested. C128 is supported by previous work from the authors. The differential effect on maternal vs. paternal X-chromosomes is observed but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between the proposed models.

results.result: Background knowledge on X-inactivation and PRC2 function. Imprinted X-inactivation silences the paternal X-chromosome in early mouse embryos, involves Xist RNA expression and coating, and is associated with PRC2 recruitment and H3K27me3 deposition. Previous work showed that Eed-/- embryos fail to maintain but properly initiate imprinted X-inactivation, potentially due to inherited maternal EED protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C31 represent established knowledge and previous findings, all supported by appropriate citations. These claims provide the scientific context for the current study and are well-documented in the literature. The hypothesis that maternal EED protein explains the proper initiation of X-inactivation in Eed-/- embryos (C27-C28) is tested in the current study.

results.result: Wild-type E3.5 blastocyst embryos show sex-specific patterns of EED, H3K27me3, and Xist RNA accumulation. Females display coincident accumulation in 72-100% of nuclei, while males lack such enrichment. There is no bias in sex ratio or genotype distribution in embryos from Eed+/- x Eedfl/-;Prm-Cre crosses.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by IF/FISH data in Figure 1A, showing expected patterns consistent with imprinted X-inactivation. C36 is supported by PCR genotyping data (Figure 1C) showing no statistical difference in genotype distribution (p>0.05). These results validate the experimental system and provide baseline controls for subsequent experiments.

results.result: Published work shows that H3K27me3 marks the Xist locus in oocytes, and injection of the H3K27me3 demethylase Kdm6b leads to derepression of maternal Xist and inactivation of both X-chromosomes in female embryos, which is expected to cause lethality.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 accurately describe published findings from other groups (Zheng et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2017; Gayen et al., 2015). These claims provide important context supporting the model that maternal PRC2 represses the maternal Xist locus. The citations are appropriate and the descriptions are consistent with the cited work.

results.result: Randomization of X-inactivation in Eedm-/- females persists in extraembryonic tissues, and male blastocysts also extinguish ectopic Xist. A concurrent publication (Inoue et al., 2018) reported random X-inactivation in extraembryonic tissues of Eed maternal-null embryos but did not demonstrate when the switch occurs or test the effect of zygotic Eed loss.
results.evaluation: C121 states that data are not shown, making it impossible to evaluate. C122 is supported by allele-specific Xist FISH (Figure 6B). C142 is speculative. C143-C145 accurately describe and critique a concurrent publication. The lack of shown data for C121 is a significant limitation, as persistence in extraembryonic tissues is an important aspect of the phenotype.

results.result: Summary of main findings: Maternal-null but not zygotic-null Eed embryos show ectopic maternal X-inactivation followed by random X-inactivation. The effect is exacerbated in Eedmz-/- embryos. Xist dynamics in Eedm-/- embryos resemble human embryos, which lack maternal PRC2. Maternal PRC2 expression may dictate the occurrence of imprinted X-inactivation in mammals.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C9 and C112 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript. The conclusions are appropriately qualified (e.g., 'may dictate' in C9) where mechanistic details remain to be established. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence (genetic, molecular, and comparative) strongly supports these conclusions.
